title: Sleep Applications
subtitle: Training arousal or sensorimotor rhythms alongside sleep care
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating sleep applications within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain sleep applications without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in sleep applications.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to sleep applications.

sections.explainSimply: Some protocols aim to improve sleep onset, continuity or subjective sleep quality.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Sleep complaints require differential assessment for circadian issues, breathing disorders, restless legs, medication effects, mood and behaviour.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: SMR and other protocols have preliminary support in some studies, but evidence does not replace sleep medicine evaluation or CBT-I when indicated.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Testing a treatment hypothesis: improvement must be meaningful, measured and compared with plausible alternatives.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand sleep applications to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not train through untreated sleep apnoea or unexplained daytime sleepiness.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using sleep applications predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not train through untreated sleep apnoea or unexplained daytime sleepiness. Evidence classification: promising in selected contexts; limited evidence.
